**Distributed Collaboration between Industry and University Partners in Higher Education**

Erik Bohemia*, Neil Smith**, Kerry Harman***, Trevor Duncan****, Chris Turnock*****, and Sung-Gul Hwang******

* School of Design, Northumbria University, Newcastle upon Tyne, NE1 8ST, United Kingdom, erik.bohemia@northumbria.ac.uk
** School of Design, Northumbria University, Newcastle upon Tyne, NE1 8ST, United Kingdom, neil.smith@northumbria.ac.uk
*** Centre for Excellence in Teaching & Learning in Assessment for Learning, Northumbria University, Newcastle upon Tyne, NE1 8ST, United Kingdom, kerry.harman@northumbria.ac.uk
**** School of Design, Northumbria University, Newcastle upon Tyne, NE1 8ST, United Kingdom
***** LTech, Northumbria University, Newcastle upon Tyne, NE1 8ST, United Kingdom, chris.turnock@northumbria.ac.uk
****** Consumer Experience Design Mobile Devices, Motorola Korea Hibrand Yangjaedong 215, Seochogu, Seoul, Korea, sung-gul.hwang@motorola.com

*Abstract*: The School of Design has been pioneering an inventive approach to curriculum structure and instruction, known as the 'Global Studio', over the last three years. This initiative marks a collaborative effort between Northumbria University and counterparts across international academic institutions and industries located in the UK, USA, Netherlands, and Korea, fostering research-informed learning and teaching. The primary goals of the Global Studio are strategically aligned with evolving industry demands, particularly transformations within the organization of product and service development. These shifts underscore the need to prepare design students with competencies essential for thriving in globally interconnected organizations, especially in developing intercultural communication and collaboration skills. This paper will center on the Global Studio as it unfolded in 2008, involving participants from Northumbria University (UK), Hongik University (Korea), Auburn University (USA), Intel (USA), Motorola's design studios in the UK and Korea, and Great Southern Wood (USA). These initiatives serve as case studies to explore the challenges and rewards associated with international, industry-focused collaborative projects executed in distributed environments.

*Key words*: Global Studio; Industry-Based Projects; International Collaboration.
Over the past three years, the School of Design at Northumbria University has been exploring an innovative curriculum design and delivery model called ‘the Global Studio’. This Global Studio initiative is a teaching and learning collaboration informed by research and involves cooperation between Northumbria University and international universities, along with industry partners. Institutions participating in this initiative include TU Delft, Napier University, Hongik University, Ohio State University, Auburn University, and RMIT University, as well as companies like Intel Corp., Motorola, Great Southern Wood, and Inverness Medical Innovation, spread across the UK, USA, Netherlands, Australia, and Korea. The objectives of the Global Studio are closely aligned with both current and future industry needs, especially those arising from shifts in how products and services are developed. These evolving demands underscore the necessity for design students to acquire skills suited for working in globally networked environments, with a particular emphasis on honing intercultural communication and collaboration skills. This paper focuses on the Global Studio conducted in 2008. It will briefly overview the collaborative projects carried out between Northumbria University and its industry partners located in the USA and Korea. We will then explore the interactions and communication among the project teams. Our analysis draws on evaluation data collected from UK-based students while the projects were ongoing and upon their completion. The insights of two authors involved in the Global Studio’s delivery are also included in the data set.
The initial concept of the Global Studio was as a course held yearly among participating universities in various countries. One of its primary goals was to create an educational setting where students could hone skills in cross-cultural communication and teamwork, all while being cost-effective enough for an entire class of students to join. Another objective was to establish a framework that allowed each partner university to independently handle teaching and assessment, thus addressing some of the challenges of cross-institutional collaborations [1]. In the first course, the roles and activities assigned to students were designed to promote engagement in communication and interaction across institutions. This was mainly accomplished by having students assume both client and designer roles. A comprehensive account of how these roles were organized has been documented elsewhere [1].

A year later, a new program within the School of Design adopted the Global Studio, with the idea that it would not only foster collaboration with university partners but also enable partnerships with industry professionals located in different regions. The inclusion of these industry partners presented new challenges compared to those faced in the earlier Global Studio. For instance, involving industry partners added layers of complexity to the communication and interactions among students, lecturers, and the partners (see Figure 1 and Figure 2).

Figure 1. Dynamics between student teams and lecturers in the Global Studio conducted in 20072. 
Only students based in the UK filled out the project exit surveys, so the data mainly reflects insights from Northumbria University students unless otherwise mentioned. 
Note: There were several work teams situated at each partner university. 

Figure 2. Enhanced complexity of interactions among student teams, industry partners, and lecturers in the Global Studio conducted in 20082. 

The introduction of three industry partners also influenced the organization of projects as well as student roles and activities. For instance, during the 2008 Global Studio, the industry partners assumed the roles of clients. As a result, students from different universities no longer acted as ‘clients’ and ‘designers’ for one another, as was done in the previous Global Studio. This greatly altered how students from the participating universities interacted and communicated with each other.
In this section, we'll provide a brief overview of the industry-related projects undertaken during the 2008 Global Studio. The Global Studio introduced three collaborative industry projects: 'Constructing Constructs,' 'Thinking Outside the Box,' and 'On the Move.' Each project was developed with various industry and university partners (refer to Table 1). The 'Constructing Constructs' initiative occurred between Northumbria University and Korea's Hong-ik University, collaborating with Motorola’s UK and Korean design studios. Motorola’s Korean Design office also contributed a staff member who taught an elective class to 10 third-year industrial design students at the participating Korean university. This industry-based project delved into two sub-themes: 'Constructing Luxury' and 'Constructing Technology' [3]. 

The second project, 'Thinking Outside the Box,' was a collaboration between UK and USA universities and Great Southern Wood (USA), a national USA timber company. The students involved were final-year industrial design students at Auburn University (USA), and the project was organized by an Auburn-based lecturer. The 'On the Move' project was commissioned by Intel, a major semiconductor company. It was conducted between Northumbria University and Intel's office in the USA. This project explored three broad themes: 'Design for Experience,' 'Imagining a Notebook,' and 'Futures of Mobile Computing.' A class of 34 third-year Industrial Design students from Northumbria University participated in all these projects, choosing which one they wanted to focus on. Ten opted for the 'On the Move' project, 12 for 'Thinking Outside the Box,' and another 12 for 'Constructing Constructs.' Additionally, several Master of Design students observed these projects as part of their Design Management studies. Even though they weren't directly designing, undergraduate students appreciated their presence, considering them 'a wealth of knowledge.' 

Furthermore, each project group was divided into smaller work teams. There were six teams at each university working on 'Thinking Outside the Box.' The 'Constructing Constructs' project involved three interconnected work teams at each participating university.

Students working on 'On the Move' developed individual concepts but were encouraged to collaborate in pairs at different stages of the design process, like idea generation. This group also presented as a collective to the industry partner, rather than making individual pitches.
The 'On the Move' project kicked off when an industry representative visited Northumbria University to introduce the project team to three main sub-themes: 'Design for Experience,' 'Imagining a Notebook,' and 'Futures of Mobile Computing.' Each sub-theme was meant to address a different timeline for potential design solutions. 'Design for Experience' focused on solutions applicable to the present day, 'Imagining a Notebook' set its sights four years into the future, and 'Futures of Mobile Computing' stretched beyond that four-year horizon. Students were encouraged to interpret these themes and submit briefs, which were then reviewed with industry representatives. The only stipulation was that any device proposed could not have a screen smaller than what the company specified. Throughout the project's timeline, the 'On the Move' industry partners frequently visited Northumbria University for in-person meetings and project evaluations. The sub-themes outlined by the Motorola representative were organized into two larger themes: 'New Luxury' (Constructing Luxury) and 'New Digital Lifestyle' (Constructing Technology). A teleconference was arranged to link UK and Korean universities with industry partner representatives, offering a briefing session along with a presentation. The industry representative's sole request was to avoid designing phones, which initially puzzled team members, as they assumed the project would relate to the company's mobile phone portfolio. Once more, student groups were tasked with developing a design brief focused on one of the two sub-themes. For the 'Thinking Outside the Box' project, a lecturer at Auburn University conducted the briefing session, as this industry project was organized by him. Students from Northumbria University were paired with their counterparts at Auburn University. UK students needed to create a design brief that would align with their USA partners’ efforts.
After the briefing sessions, students were asked to share an introductory post and a photo of themselves on the project wiki pages. The next task for the teams was to establish a collaborative environment that included: (i) creating a wiki page, (ii) choosing a team name, (iii) designing a logo, and then (iv) uploading design briefs to their team project wiki pages. This was followed by a virtual meeting with other partners to discuss these design briefs. Once the briefs were finalized, teams embarked on research to explore solutions to the design challenges. The research outcomes were analyzed to guide the development of concepts, which were further reviewed to direct subsequent improvements and revisions of the design proposals. Eventually, this process culminated in the presentation of the final design proposals to the industry partner representatives. The format of these presentations varied among the project teams and within individual teams. For instance, the ‘On the Move’ final design presentations comprised a series of two-minute animations that highlighted the key benefits of each design concept, compiled into a standalone DVD presentation. The ‘Constructing Constructs’ project combined storyboards and multimedia animations. Meanwhile, ‘Thinking Outside the Box’ used storyboards and scale models to demonstrate the working principles of different design proposals. The three projects employed a range of communication tools to facilitate both asynchronous and synchronous interactions. The choice of these tools depended on the available communication technology at each participating organization and the IT policies of the UK-based university. Students had the chance to work both in the same location and distributed environments and to interact using a variety of communication technologies while engaging in asynchronous and synchronous communications. For example, they worked together in the same location and communicated in real-time with team members based at the same institution (top left quadrant in Figure 3). Figure 3 Dimensions of collaboration [based on 4] These team members also utilized asynchronous communication tools, such as email and wiki pages (top right quadrant in Figure 3). They collaborated across distances and communicated synchronously through tele/videoconferencing with partners in other locations (bottom left quadrant in Figure 3). Asynchronous tools like email and wiki pages were used to communicate with partners situated in other geographical areas (bottom right quadrant in Figure 3).
To facilitate asynchronous communication, each project was given access to secured, dedicated wiki pages using MediaWiki software. These wikis were hosted by Northumbria University. The selection of wiki pages as a communication tool was based on several reasons:

- External collaborators could access these dedicated project wikis, unlike the existing university online learning system, Blackboard, which was limited to enrolled students and university staff.   
- Users, upon receiving their individual log-ins, could freely create, edit, and link pages, offering them flexibility in organizing their group or individual project wikis.  
- Basic text editing capabilities within wikis meant that knowledge of HTML wasn’t necessary, and standard files could be uploaded directly, eliminating the need for special external software like web editors or FTP clients. 

The goal was for the design teams to upload various elements of their work—such as design briefs, research including mind maps and mood boards, videos, sketches, and other visual representations of design concepts, storyboards, and multimedia files like animations and movies—onto their group or individual project wiki pages. During scheduled synchronous project meetings, participants could view these pages at each site, permitting them to present and discuss the project using the material accessible on the wiki pages.
Even though all students participated in the introductory exercise, many grappled with using the wiki pages. Some opted not to use them at all, particularly those attending Auburn University. Instead, they chose Facebook over the designated project wiki pages for asynchronous communication with their UK counterparts. Consequently, the students in the UK involved in the 'Thinking Outside the Box' project also gravitated towards using Facebook instead of the wiki pages. One UK student noted: "I enjoyed the video/teleconferencing experience, as it gave me new skills and boosted my confidence in presenting my ideas through various mediums. The student I worked with didn’t use the wiki pages, though I kept asking. So, I didn’t contribute much because it felt pointless." Meanwhile, students in the USA reported difficulties with accidentally overwriting others’ wiki pages, files, and images, as echoed in a student's feedback: "The wiki page was a hassle. Uploading images was a nightmare. Our class wasn't familiar with the system, and many students misplaced pages and overwrote others’ work." This occurred due to the 'flat' structure of wiki pages, unlike HTML-based web pages with folders. This required each new wiki page and uploaded files or images to have unique names to avoid overwriting existing content. For instance, a student might upload a photo titled ‘my photo.jpg’, only for another to upload an image with the same name, ignoring the warning message indicating an existing file with the same name. If they proceeded, the original image would be overwritten, unnoticed unless they checked the other person’s wiki pages. Students expressed widespread dissatisfaction with the wikis' poor editing capabilities, inadequate file uploading features, and slow upload speeds. To combat these issues, student teams working on the ‘Constructing Constructs’ project uploaded large multimedia files to ‘free’ file-sharing sites, then shared links on their project wiki pages so others could access the files. However, this led to new challenges. For one, the project files were no longer stored in a secure project web environment, raising concerns about confidentiality breaches. Additionally, these links often expired within a few days, and many free file-sharing sites displayed ads for adult content or software that might harm a visitor’s computer. Despite the problems with wiki pages, students found the concept of a shared web space for project progress beneficial, as one student remarked: "Wiki pages can be tricky to grasp, but they’re handy for sharing ideas and work." They also appreciated having their work (like multimedia files) accessible online to other student teams and industry partners, which facilitated explaining their ideas over the phone or videoconference. Observing other students' work was insightful, as another student noted: "It was good to see how everyone tackles the project uniquely—we can compare our learning methods." The ability to observe and be observed by others also introduced a competitive edge, exemplified by this student's comment: "It pushes you to reach your potential as you see real competition. Engaging with others enhances your work."
During the 2008 Global Studio sessions, a UK university had IT policies that blocked all messaging and Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) software. This restriction prevented participants from that university from using internet-based applications like AOL Messenger, MSN Messenger, Yahoo! Messenger, Net Meeting, ooVoo, and Skype for real-time communication through the university’s IT network. As a result, students and academics couldn't use these tools for synchronous interactions with their external collaborators. Instead, they relied on standard phones or videoconferencing equipment for real-time communication. Teleconferencing was the primary method for supporting synchronous discussions in the 'Constructing Constructs' and 'On the Move' projects, with industry partners providing the resources and setting up these sessions. Typically, these teleconferences could last two hours or longer and cost around £100 each. For instance, a representative from Motorola based in the UK would arrange a three-way teleconference bridge for meetings involving universities in the UK and Korea, and this industry partner. Both UK and USA universities had access to regular videoconferencing equipment, enabling frequent video meetings between their teams. Due to the reliance on university phones and videoconferencing gear, these synchronous meetings had to be planned well ahead by lecturers and industry partners. This logistical requirement meant that UK-based students could not engage in spontaneous discussions with their external counterparts unless they were willing to pay for expensive personal phone calls. Teams using teleconferencing along with wikis for synchronous discussions, such as those on the 'Constructing Constructs' and 'On the Move' projects, expressed a preference for videoconferencing. They felt it would have helped them explain their ideas and showcase their concepts more effectively. They also noted issues with the sound quality of speakerphones. Conversely, teams on the 'Thinking Outside the Box' project, which mainly used videoconferencing without relying on project wikis to share progress, found it challenging to see concepts clearly during video meetings. The 'On the Move' teams had several face-to-face interactions with industry partners throughout the project's duration (refer to Table 3). Interestingly, only one student explicitly acknowledged the value of these meetings. The use and availability of communication technologies led to differences in the methods project teams employed during their work (refer to Table 2). 

Table 2 outlines the communication technologies used by each project:

Every industry-based project commenced in February. Interestingly, the "On the Move" project concluded 2 ½ months later than the other two. Table 3 outlines the frequency of communication meetings for each project and their duration. It also highlights the technology used for communication and the involvement of industry partners. For instance, industry partners participated in all communication sessions for the "Constructing the Construct" and "On the Move" projects. Conversely, the industry partner for "Thinking Outside the Box" only joined the UK-based workgroups in the latter half of the project. Notably, only this project's workgroups utilized videoconferencing for meetings. The "On the Move" teams held nine meetings with industry partners over 20 weeks, including four face-to-face meetings when U.S.-based industry staff visited the UK project team. The "Constructing the Construct" teams conducted seven meetings with university and industry partners during the 10-week project period. Meanwhile, the "Thinking Outside the Box" teams also held seven meetings, most via videoconferencing, but the UK teams included the industry partner in only two sessions.

Overall, students involved in "Thinking Outside the Box" rated their experience as less satisfying compared to those in the other projects. Their scores were lower in how well each project phase was executed (e.g., Writing a design brief, Communicating design concepts, Design progress reviews, and Presenting the final design proposal). However, over 80% of students on the other projects rated these phases as "very well" or "well." Even students from "Thinking Outside the Box" acknowledged that the Global Studio enhanced their distance communication skills and shed light on the difficulties of distributed communication, as shown by comments such as: - Realizing how hard it is to communicate across countries. - Using Wiki pages and videoconferencing for the first time, I now understand why it's so challenging! Similar sentiments were shared by students in the other groups. All three project groups noted increased confidence in presenting ideas publicly and using various communication technologies. For instance, a student from "On the Move" remarked on their increased confidence in discussing ideas with people from different countries. Another stated they gained more confidence with communication skills due to weekly meetings. Across the board, students felt that the course bolstered their skills in remote communication, with many acknowledging that the Global Studio deepened their understanding of challenges faced when working with distributed design teams or clients. Korean students specifically mentioned that the Global Studio was an opportunity to practice and enhance their English language skills. Many students expressed a positive view of their learning experiences, acknowledging the knowledge gained through participation in the Global Studio, with comments like: - Experiencing the project first-hand gave me everything, from open mindset to confidence and embracing challenges. - Learned how easily miscommunications can happen online. - It was challenging to communicate online without body language. - Realized the difficulties of long-distance communication. - Improved communication skills across various media. - Engaging with a real client and Korean students enhanced teamwork. - Compelled to articulate everything online and on the spot, I improved my communication skills. - I observed how reliant I am on verbal explanation and speech.
Students overall expressed that engaging in the Global Studio was an enjoyable learning experience. They unanimously agreed that collaborating with international universities and industry partners enhanced their communication skills. Nevertheless, feedback also highlighted challenges with communication technologies, particularly the difficulty in using wiki pages. A study titled 'The Great Expectations of ICT' examined first-year students' interactions with ICT in the UK Higher Education sector and found that students were unfamiliar and uncomfortable with wiki pages. The report underscores that this technology currently pushes students "beyond their comfort zones." Insights from the Global Studio suggest that students would benefit from better training and accessible tutorials on using wiki pages throughout the project. Alternatively, exploring user-friendly external wiki editors could make editing simpler. The academic team at Northumbria University is collaborating with IT systems and Learning Technology staff to determine necessary support for improving interactions and communications among distributed Global Studio teams. This multidisciplinary research team is investigating technologies to enable student groups to initiate teleconferences and/or videoconferences with counterparts at other universities. Data indicates that frequent videoconferencing between UK and USA student teams did not significantly increase student satisfaction. These students reported the lowest satisfaction on most indicators in both progress and exit surveys. Another factor might be that the industry partner involved in this project didn’t begin interaction with the UK-based teams until the mid-project progress review. From the lecturers' perspective, managing three industry projects was complex. To simplify communication and management, only one industry project will proceed in the subsequent Global Studio. In conclusion, we suggest that the Global Studio offers students a rich learning environment by exposing them to the complexities of communication and project management through design projects in distributed settings alongside international university and industry partners.
We extend our heartfelt thanks to our industry partners for their generous support, as well as to the academics and students who participated. We appreciate Nick Oakley and Patrick Lynch from the Intel Mobility Group, Jerry Wright from Great Southern Wood Preserving, Inc., and Tsai Lu Liu from Auburn University. Our gratitude also goes to Nicholas Jinkinson from the Motorola UK Design Centre and Ja-Sung Koo from the Motorola/Consumer eXperience Design team in Seoul, Korea.
